scope: All seven files read and compared with prototype requirements; targeted primary-source checks only, not verification of every citation or an amplifier validation. Originals preserved.

rules.first_line: Specify the intended behavior: clean hi-fi reproduction, clean guitar headroom, deliberate overdrive, or a combination. Do not automatically treat a desirable guitar distortion characteristic as good hi-fi performance.
Define output power together with load, frequency range, and distortion limit. A wattage figure alone is an incomplete design target.
Choose the output tubes, operating voltages, bias, and output transformer together. They are interdependent, not independent shopping decisions.
Distinguish topology from operating class. Push-pull does not automatically mean Class AB, and cathode bias does not automatically mean Class A.
Use a mains-isolated power supply. For your build, specify 220 V, 50 Hz input compatibility for every mains-powered supply, including any separate control supply.
Give protective earth a dedicated, mechanically secure chassis connection. Never switch, fuse, or disconnect protective earth to cure hum. Audio grounding is a separate design problem.

Specify fuses properly: current, time characteristic, voltage, breaking capacity, and location. Check whether secondary faults can bypass the protection; never casually copy a 120 V amplifier’s fuse value.

Provide discharge paths for stored high voltage. Check every capacitor bank and switch position. A bleeder resistor or extinguished indicator is not proof that the circuit is discharged—verify with appropriately rated equipment.
Rate switches for the actual circuit they interrupt. A mains AC rating does not automatically establish suitability for several hundred volts DC.

Determine insulation spacing from actual requirements. Working voltage, transients, insulation category, board material, contamination, and altitude matter; there is no universal “tube-amp clearance” number.
Use the exact tube manufacturer’s datasheet. Verify pinout, heater requirements, voltage limits, dissipation, grid-circuit resistance, and heater-to-cathode limits.
Do not assume tubes sharing a socket are interchangeable. Even common nine-pin dual triodes can have different heater connections.
Calculate idle plate dissipation using plate-to-cathode voltage:
Check dissipation throughout the output range—not only at idle or full power. In Class AB, the worst operating point can occur between them.
Do not use “70% bias” as a universal design rule. Safe bias depends on operating voltage, reflected load, tube characteristics, and operating class.

Treat screen-grid dissipation separately. Safe plate dissipation does not guarantee safe screens, particularly during overdrive. Size screen resistors for current limiting, heat, and fault-voltage stress.
Give every control grid a defined DC return path. Check normal operation, switching transitions, disconnected controls, and broken potentiometer wipers.
Respect the maximum grid-circuit resistance. Include the relevant grid stopper, grid-leak resistor, and bias-source resistance—not merely the resistor labelled “grid leak.”
Make adjustable fixed bias fail toward a colder operating point. Limit the adjustment range and address loss of wiper contact.
Check bias during startup, shutdown, and rapid power cycling. Power tubes must not remain conducting with substantial B+ but inadequate negative bias.
Do not treat cathode bias as automatic protection. Verify resistor dissipation, bypass-capacitor stress, current sharing, and behavior under sustained drive.
Match reflected primary impedance to the operating point. The transformer reflects the connected speaker load:
Do not confuse winding DC resistance with rated audio impedance. A resistance-meter reading is not the transformer’s specified primary load.
Specify bass performance at the required output power. A transformer that handles its rated watts at guitar frequencies may not handle the same power at deep hi-fi bass frequencies.

Use a transformer suitable for the DC operating conditions. Conventional single-ended stages need DC-current capability and an appropriate core gap; push-pull stages require attention to current imbalance.

Account for plate swings above B+. Insulation and component ratings must accommodate signal peaks and inductive transients. Do not drive the amplifier without its intended load unless unloaded operation has been specifically protected and validated.
Budget gain and headroom stage by stage. Decide which stage should clip first; include losses from tone controls, mixers, effects loops, and feedback.
Account for loading between stages. Tone controls and volume pots affect the preceding stage’s gain, frequency response, and available signal swing.
Calculate coupling-capacitor behavior using the actual surrounding circuit. Larger capacitors are not automatically better; excessively low-frequency response can be undesirable.
Control blocking distortion. Grid current can charge coupling capacitors and temporarily shift bias; assess recovery after hard clipping, not just the clipped waveform.
Put grid stoppers close to the tube’s grid pin. Long wiring after the resistor undermines parasitic-oscillation suppression. Choose values for stability, overload behavior, and bandwidth together.
Give the phase inverter adequate loaded output swing. Balance alone is insufficient: check drive capability and clipping behavior with the actual power-tube grid networks attached.
Design for high mains and light-load/startup voltage. B+ can rise before the tubes conduct; normal warm operating voltage is not the worst-case capacitor voltage.
Do not equate transformer AC current with available DC current. Capacitor-input rectifiers draw charging pulses that increase winding RMS current and heating.
Match reservoir capacitance to the rectifier and transformer. More capacitance increases charging stress; tube rectifiers have specific reservoir-capacitance and source-resistance requirements.
Give sensitive stages suitable supply decoupling. Filtering must suppress ripple and prevent stages from coupling through their shared supply.
For series electrolytics, check voltage sharing and reduced capacitance. Design balancing resistors from capacitor leakage and operating conditions, and verify their voltage and power ratings.
Do not add standby circuitry by habit. Define its purpose, switching stress, discharge behavior, and effect on bias. A standby switch is not a substitute for correctly rated components.
Check heater voltage at the sockets under load, across the intended mains range—not only at the transformer terminals.
Budget all heater current, including added reverb tubes and indicators. Rectified DC heater supplies require extra transformer-current allowance.
Give the heater supply one deliberate reference scheme. Avoid floating heaters and conflicting references on opposite sides of a rectifier.
Check heater-to-cathode voltage for every stage, including startup. Cathode followers and elevated-cathode circuits may require heater elevation or separate windings.
Keep heater current loops small. Twist AC heater pairs and separate them from sensitive signal wiring. DC heaters must actually be clean; poorly filtered DC can introduce noise.
Design current-return paths—not just ground symbols. Do not let the chassis become an accidental shared signal-return conductor.
Keep rectifier charging currents out of input-stage returns. Place the rectifier–reservoir loop compactly and route its return deliberately.
Ground each stage with its associated local supply-decoupling return. Prevent output-stage and control-circuit currents from sharing sensitive input paths.
Separate low-level inputs from large-signal outputs. Short grid wiring and sensible stage placement help prevent unintended feedback.
Plan chassis connections at jacks, pots, shields, and mounting hardware. Accidental additional connections can defeat an otherwise sound grounding scheme.
Verify feedback polarity with the actual transformer connections. Incorrect phasing can turn intended negative feedback into positive feedback.
Validate stability beyond the audible band. An amplifier can sound normal while suffering ultrasonic oscillation.
Test feedback with realistic reactive loads and control extremes. Presence, resonance, feedback switches, and output-tap changes can alter loop behavior.
Do not assume more feedback is always better. It changes gain, distortion, output impedance, clipping behavior, and stability requirements.
Check voltage ratings as well as wattage. Screen resistors, plate resistors, and supply-dropping resistors may face startup or fault stresses far beyond their normal dissipation.
Design for the temperature inside the finished enclosure. Keep heat-sensitive components away from tubes and hot resistors; validate after the amplifier reaches operating temperature.
Verify every symbol-to-footprint pin mapping against the physical part. Include tube-socket viewing direction, transformer leads, switched jacks, and relay contact states.
Never defeat oscilloscope protective earth. Ordinary bench-scope ground clips are generally earth-referenced; use properly rated differential or isolated measurement equipment where required.

Test before relying on listening impressions. Use a suitably rated resistive dummy load for power measurements, then validate reactive-load stability, clipping recovery, hum, temperature, bias drift, and startup/shutdown behavior. Record expected voltages and test conditions.
Match the reverb tank, driver, and transformer as a system. Tank impedance is frequency-dependent; the driver needs adequate current, not merely voltage gain.
Protect the reverb driver against an unplugged tank and flyback transients. Keep its transformer away from magnetic hum sources and its low-level recovery wiring away from the driver.

Keep the external footswitch interface touch-safe and low voltage. Specify relay isolation and switching ratings; separately address debounce, audio-pop suppression, coil transients, startup defaults, and TRS insertion shorts. Debouncing alone does not make audio switching quiet.

Start with the enclosure. Establish the board outline, mounting holes, connector positions, component heights, and cable access before routing.
Allow space around components. Include connector plugs, screwdrivers, heatsinks, and insertion/removal clearance—not just the component body. [1]
Check every footprint against the actual part. Verify pad numbering, lead pitch, finished-hole size, body dimensions, polarity, and top-view versus bottom-view drawings.
Never trust a footprint merely because its name matches. This is especially important for downloaded or AI-generated libraries, connectors, transistors, and tube sockets. [2]
Choose the manufacturer’s capabilities before setting design rules. Check trace/space limits, hole sizes, annular rings, copper thickness, solder mask, and board-edge clearances. [3]
Choose the layer stack deliberately. Give critical signals a nearby, continuous reference plane; do not select layers solely according to routing convenience. [4]
Group components by function. Keep each amplifier stage, regulator, interface, and associated support components together.
Separate noise sources from sensitive circuits. Switching power supplies and high-current paths should not occupy the same area as low-level analog inputs. [5]
Place the most layout-sensitive components first. Examples include switching-power components, oscillator parts, feedback networks, and bypass capacitors.
Follow the component manufacturer’s recommended layout. A correct schematic does not make an arbitrary placement electrically equivalent. [6]
Put electrostatic-discharge protection at the connector. Route the incoming signal through the protection location before it reaches the vulnerable circuit.
Give protection devices a short discharge-return path. A nearby protection diode with a long, inductive ground connection can still provide poor protection. [7]
Ground is not an ideal zero-voltage surface. Shared return impedance lets one circuit’s current disturb another circuit’s reference. [5]
Prefer a continuous ground plane within each non-isolated domain. Separate noisy and quiet functions through placement and current-path control—not automatic plane splitting.
Do not route fast signals across ground-plane gaps. The return current must detour, increasing loop area and interference.
Check return paths whenever a signal changes layers. When it changes between ground reference planes, provide a nearby stitching via connecting those planes.
Keep heavy and pulsed returns out of sensitive reference paths. Rectifier, speaker, and power-stage currents should not share a narrow return section with an input stage.
Use star or bus grounding deliberately—not universally. These can suit audio power systems, but “everything must connect to one distant star” is not a universal PCB rule. [8]
Place bypass capacitors electrically close to their supply pins. Physical proximity is insufficient when the connecting traces take a long detour.
Minimize the complete bypass loop. Consider the capacitor, supply pin, device return, and ground connection together.
Keep bypass connections short and low-inductance. Avoid long, thin traces between the capacitor and the pins it serves.
Do not expect one distant bulk capacitor to replace local bypassing. Bulk energy storage and high-frequency decoupling serve different needs. [5]
Follow the device’s specified capacitor placement and connections. Particular regulators and isolated supplies can require capacitors directly between designated supply-and-return pin pairs. [9]
Avoid unnecessary shared bottlenecks in power distribution. Separate noisy branches and provide their local decoupling rather than feeding everything through one restrictive path. [10]
Route critical nets before ordinary control signals. Preserve the geometry needed by clocks, feedback, sensitive inputs, and controlled-impedance connections.
Keep sensitive traces short and away from aggressors. Long parallel runs increase opportunities for coupling.
Judge digital routing by edge speed—not merely clock frequency. A slowly repeating signal can still have very fast transitions.
Calculate controlled impedance using the actual stack-up. Trace width alone does not determine impedance.
Route differential pairs consistently. Maintain the required width, spacing, reference continuity, and reasonably symmetric transitions.
Match lengths only to an actual timing requirement. Avoid adding unnecessary meanders or stubs merely to make traces look equal. [4]
Keep amplifier feedback networks compact. Unintended capacitance at sensitive input nodes can alter stability; copper beneath those nodes may need a deliberate keepout. [11]
Size traces for current, copper thickness, temperature rise, and voltage drop. There is no universally correct “power trace width.”
Check vias as well as traces. A wide trace feeding a single small via can still create an electrical and thermal bottleneck. [12]
Identify the switching hot loop. Minimize the loop carrying rapidly changing current; its location depends on the converter topology.
Keep switching-node copper controlled. Use enough for current and heat, but do not turn a rapidly switching node into an unnecessarily large copper area.
Keep gate-drive loops compact. Route the drive and its return together; do not consider only the gate trace.
Keep feedback and sensing away from switching nodes. Short routing is not an improvement when it passes through a noisy region. [10]
Use Kelvin connections for current sensing. Run separate sense traces from the intended shunt measurement points, rather than measuring through current-carrying copper. [13]
Design the heat-removal path, not just the electrical connection. Power parts may depend on copper area and thermal vias to reach their intended performance.
Treat thermal reliefs as a trade-off. They improve solderability but can restrict current and heat flow; do not apply them indiscriminately to power connections. [10]
Check exposed-pad electrical connections. Follow the exact datasheet; exposed metal and thermal structures are not automatically interchangeable with ground.
Respect package-specific keepouts. Some packages contain exposed structures that must not contact PCB copper. [6]
Keep precision analog circuits away from thermal gradients. Uneven heating can create measurement errors even when the electrical routing looks correct. [14]
Distinguish clearance from creepage. Clearance is the shortest distance through air; creepage is the shortest path along an insulating surface.
Do not choose safety spacing from nominal voltage alone. Consider working voltage, transients, insulation category, pollution degree, material, altitude, and the applicable equipment standard. [15]
Check the whole assembled insulation boundary. Include pads, solder, component leads, connectors, mounting hardware, and nearby accessible metal—not just trace spacing.
Do not assume a board slot solves every spacing problem. A slot can increase PCB creepage without increasing air clearance or the creepage across a component.
Do not casually credit solder mask or coating as safety insulation. Any claimed reduction in required spacing needs an appropriately qualified insulation/coating system. [16]
Keep protective earth separate from noise-control decisions. For a Class I metal-chassis build, use a secure dedicated chassis bond; never remove protective earth to cure hum. [8]
Check solder-mask openings and the mask between adjacent pads. Copper clearances alone do not guarantee a manufacturable solder-mask pattern.
Specify via treatment deliberately. Tented, open, filled, and capped vias are not equivalent manufacturing instructions. [17]
Make polarity and pin 1 unmistakable. Ensure markings remain useful when the part is installed.
Keep identification readable and off soldering surfaces. Reference designators and connector labels should not disappear beneath components or overlap exposed pads. [2]
Provide accessible test points on important nets. Include supplies, returns, and diagnostic signals; allow room for the actual probe.
Plan test access around the assembled board. Tall components, heatsinks, and enclosure hardware must not block the points you need to reach. [18]
Set meaningful net classes and custom rules. High-voltage, high-current, ordinary signal, and controlled-impedance nets should not all inherit unsuitable defaults.
Refill every copper zone before checking the board. Inspect for disconnected islands, narrow connections, and unintentionally interrupted return paths.
Run design-rule checking and schematic-to-PCB parity checking. Resolve unintended shorts, unconnected items, clearance violations, and schematic mismatches.
Review exclusions instead of hiding problems. Every waived violation should have an understood, documented reason.
Inspect the exported manufacturing files. Check copper, solder mask, drill data, board outline, and layer selection—not just the editor view.
Treat a clean DRC as necessary, not sufficient. It checks configured rules; it does not establish analog performance, adequate cooling, or product safety. [19]
Keep high-gain inputs away from later-stage outputs. Unintended coupling can create feedback, oscillation, or unwanted interaction between stages. [5]
Keep the connection after a grid-stopper resistor extremely short. Place it at or very near the tube’s grid connection rather than leaving a long unprotected grid lead. [20]
Route heater supply and return together. Use paired PCB routing and tightly twisted off-board AC heater wiring; keep them away from sensitive signal wiring.
Keep rectifier charging pulses local. Arrange the transformer-secondary, rectifier, and first reservoir-capacitor circuit so its pulsed current does not travel through preamp returns.
Plan grounding across the whole amplifier. Include jacks, pots, cable shields, board interconnects, and chassis connections; PCB grounding alone cannot control paths created elsewhere. [8]
